extracted.intended_audience: historians of science, evolutionary biologists, naturalists, and scholarly readers interested in Darwin's work and the development of the Origin of Species
extracted.subtask_short: writing a scientific monograph on species
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and historical exemplars for composing a comprehensive scientific monograph on species and variation, including which topics/chapters to include, types of evidence to collect, and editorial/production considerations. Grounded in Darwin's Sketch (1844), letters, and Hooker's commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open with variation under domestication and artificial selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sketch and the 'Origin' open with a chapter on variation under domestication and on artificial selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This foundation is used to introduce the main argument: domestic-breeding examples illustrate principles later applied to nature. Use domestic examples to make the argument accessible and grounded in observable cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat variation under nature and natural selection (including the struggle for life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow domestic variation with discussions on variation under nature, on natural selection, and on the struggle for life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present the mechanism (natural selection) after illustrating variation; incorporate the struggle for existence as a central explanatory principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a chapter on variation in instincts and habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter III of the Sketch treats variations in instincts and habits, corresponding to Chapter VII of the 'Origin'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place treatment of instinct early enough to prevent quick rejection by readers who think natural selection cannot act on instincts; use it to complement structural variation chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devote a section to the problem of intermediate/transition forms (intermediateness needed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter I of the second part: 'On the kind of intermediateness necessary, and the number of such intermediate forms.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include geological discussion and address objections that intermediate forms are absent; argue what degree and number of intermediates are necessary to support descent with modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss the gradual appearance and disappearance of organic beings (fossil record)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter II: 'The gradual appearance and disappearance of organic beings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat extinction and fossil succession; relate observed fossil patterns to expectations under descent and selection; address apparent gaps and rates of change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a detailed geographical distribution chapter
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter III: 'Geographical Distribution.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlate distributional patterns with historical processes (migration, transport, geological change). Hooker praises Darwin's geographical discussion as 'a perfect model of what such a paper should be.' Use island and mountain cases as tests of the theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include chapters on affinities, classification, and unity of type
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter IV: 'Affinities and Classification of Organic beings.' Chapter V: 'Unity of Type,' morphology, embryology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how descent explains affinities and classification; use morphology and embryology to support unity of type arguments and taxonomic relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat rudimentary organs explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter VI: 'Rudimentary Organs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vestigial structures as evidence of descent and historical modification; discuss their distribution and possible origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: End with recapitulation and a grand concluding statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter VII: Recapitulation and Conclusion; Darwin's final sentence echoes his earlier notebooks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize how the diverse lines of evidence fit the theory; a concluding, synthetic, and memorable sentence helps convey the theory's scope and grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use domestic animals and breeding as a central methodological exemplar
rubrics_metrics.description: The first part contains the main argument founded on the study of domestic animals; both the Sketch and the 'Origin' open with a chapter on variation under domestication and artificial selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage well-documented cases from domestication to illustrate variation, selection, and divergence as an accessible analog for natural processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address the divergence of character and its adaptive advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly discuss how lesser differences between varieties become augmented into greater differences between species (divergence of character).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain divergence via division of labour, occupation of diverse ecological 'places', and increased total numbers through complementary varieties; give analogies (e.g., mixed wheat varieties) to demonstrate population-level advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enunciate sexual selection and 'unconscious' selection principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sketch contains the first mention of the principle of Sexual Selection and the important form known as 'unconscious' selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sexual selection as a distinct mechanism of divergence and adaptation; describe non-conscious breeder effects where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the law of age-corresponding appearance of peculiarities
rubrics_metrics.description: A law that peculiarities tend to appear in the offspring at an age corresponding to that at which they occurred in the parent is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss timing of trait expression across generations and its evolutionary implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote comparative anatomy, study of instincts, heredity, hybridism, and generation
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory 'would give zest to recent and fossil comparative anatomy; it would lead to the study of instincts, heredity, and mind-heredity...and direct examination of direct passages of structure in species...hybridity and generation, causes of change.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple biological subfields as converging lines of evidence; encourage directed empirical work in these areas to test and extend the theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect extensive, diverse factual evidence from many sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin: 'I determined to collect blindly every sort of fact, which could bear any way on what are species. I have read heaps of agricultural and horticultural books, and have never ceased collecting facts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather empirical data from natural history collections, agricultural/horticultural literature, geology, museum specimens, and correspondence; annotate sources and cross-reference passages that bear on the central theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate island biogeography and compare representatives across islands
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare whether separate islands possess distinct representative species of the same genera (Galapagos, Sandwich Islands, Azores, Canary Islands, St. Helena).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study affinities of island taxa to continental taxa, habitat-level differences within islands (summit vs lowland), and the pattern of distinct representative species between islands as critical tests of dispersal and speciation hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlate geographical range with persistence in time
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin: 'I think it is pretty well established, that according as the geographical range of a species is wide, so is its persistence and duration in time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use palaeontological and biogeographical data to test whether wide-ranging species persist longer; incorporate this correlation into arguments about species longevity and extinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tackle objections about missing intermediate forms directly (use analogy and counter-examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respond to critics (e.g., Cuvier) who ask 'why have not some intermediate forms been discovered?' with analogies (e.g., 'show me every step between bulldog and greyhound') and arguments about incompleteness and extinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate demands for complete series; explain expected rarity of intermediates, patterns of extinction, and the fossil record's incompleteness; use living analogies and domestic breeds to illustrate points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include general remarks on affinities and structure to engage non-specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin regretted that Hooker's systematic paper lacked 'general remarks on affinities, structures, etc., which make them interesting even to a non-Botanist.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing technical/systematic papers, add accessible general discussion of affinities and structural significance to broaden appeal beyond specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial and publication planning for extensive manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin's letter: provide funds for an editor (400–500 pounds), choose an editor who is both a geologist and naturalist (Lyell, Forbes, Henslow, Hooker, Strickland), hand over annotated books and scrap portfolios, and allow editor discretion on interpolations and appendices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For large, complex works, plan editorial support, select editors with appropriate disciplinary breadth, provide annotated source material, and budget for time-consuming collation, copying, and correction. If no suitable editor is found, consider publishing the sketch 'as it is' with a clear statement of its provenance.
